title: The Morning Brief: Circle launches Arc, Senate kills Clarity Act, regulatory divergence spreads
dek: Circle's Arc blockchain goes live this morning with 11 Wall Street validators including BlackRock and DTCC, but the Senate's collapse of the Clarity Act yesterday means the U.S. now has no federal crypto framework while other jurisdictions move fast on settlement infrastructure and stablecoins.
author: Crypto Cronkite
key_fact: The U.S. regulatory vacuum created by yesterday's 49-50 Senate cloture failure contrasts sharply with today's Arc launch and ongoing institutional settlement moves in India and Europe, suggesting crypto infrastructure is building around the regulatory absence rather than waiting for it.
bottom_line: Circle's Arc launches today with 11 Wall Street validators as institutional settlement infrastructure spreads through India, Europe, and now permissioned PoA on Ethereum-compatible infrastructure; simultaneously, the Senate's collapse of the Clarity Act yesterday left the U.S. without federal crypto framework, a regulatory vacuum that appears to be accelerating institutional moves to build around U.S. jurisdiction rather than within it. The desk's ETF flows show BTC outflows of $450.4 million on September 15 following the Clarity Act failure, liquidating $570 million in bullish futures, while ethereum flows turned negative only this session after three prior inflow days. What to watch: Arc's real institutional settlement volume in its first weeks, whether individual validator voting weights remain concentrated or disperse before mainnet, the timeline for DTCC-custodied asset integration targeted for H2 2027, and whether Senate Republicans attempt a revised Clarity Act with stronger ethics provisions or allow the bill to remain dead through year-end.
body: Circle's Arc mainnet launches on September 16 with 11 founding validators drawn from Wall Street and payments infrastructure: BlackRock, DTCC, Visa, Mastercard, ICE, and six others. The network uses permissioned Proof-of-Authority consensus in which validators finalize blocks by two-thirds pre-commitment vote, then locks transactions irreversibly at the consensus layer. Developers can deploy applications permissionlessly, but Arc's documentation explicitly walls off validators and the network from liability for third-party applications, a structural choice designed to let custodians and settlement operators participate without crypto platform risk. The critical unresolved questions are individual validator voting weights, which remain undisclosed at launch, and whether real institutional settlement volume materializes before the ARC token's May 2028 delivery deadline.

Institutional settlement infrastructure is moving faster outside the U.S. regulatory vacuum. India's Securities and Exchange Board announced Demat 2.0 on September 10, a framework that moved ₹1,025 crore in tokenized corporate bonds through atomic delivery-versus-payment settlement between private digital tokens and Reserve Bank of India wholesale digital rupee on September 7 and 9. Three issuers, REC Limited (₹500 crore), L&T Limited (₹500 crore), and IIFL (₹25 crore), completed the first stage as a depository-controlled pilot. Retail participation and secondary-market trading are explicitly deferred to a later stage. The architecture preserves exact legal and economic terms of traditional dematerialized securities while removing settlement risk: either bond and payment both settle or neither does, eliminating windows where one side could default. Separately, Revolut began rolling out EURR, a euro-backed stablecoin issued by Bridge Building S.A. (a Stripe company and Luxembourg-regulated electronic money institution), to selected customers in Denmark, Poland, and Portugal. Bridge was authorized on June 29, 2026, and holds ₹374 in EURR in circulation as of August 25, well below Circle's EURC circulation of ₹394.5 million on the same date.

The Senate's failure to advance the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act yesterday collapsed the most substantial bipartisan crypto regulatory push in U.S. legislative history. The cloture motion fell 49-50 on September 15, one vote short of the 60 required. Four Senate Republicans, Susan Collins, Josh Hawley, Jerry Moran, and Thom Tillis, voted no alongside all Democrats. Seven Democrats who spent months negotiating the bill's final text voted against proceeding: Kirsten Gillibrand, Mark Warner, Cory Booker, Raphael Warnock, Ruben Gallego, Angela Alsobrooks, and Catherine Cortez Masto. They cited ethics provisions they said were too weak to prevent Trump and his appointees from profiting from crypto ventures while overseeing the industry. Republicans had released new ethics language late Sunday night that incorporated 126 substantive changes Democrats had sought, but staff negotiations collapsed without agreement. Per The Defiant's reporting, Senator Elissa Slotkin stated the ethics provisions were "simply too thin," and Senator Elizabeth Warren called them "a tiny little fig leaf" with multiple escape hatches: Attorney General power, Office of Government Ethics waiver authority, and blind-trust loopholes. Trump and his family had accumulated $1.4 billion from crypto ventures in 2025 alone, per Warren's remarks, and fans who bought Trump memecoins had lost nearly $4 billion. The failure ends Clarity Act prospects in 2026; revival would require reopening ethics language Republicans had presented as final.

The tape reflects regulatory disappointment and profit-taking. The desk's BTC ETF flows board shows an outflow of $450.4 million on September 15, extending a net outflow of $706.6 million over the last five sessions. ETH ETF flows tell a different story: an outflow of $142.3 million on the day, but a net inflow of $200.0 million over the last five sessions, meaning flows turned negative only this session after three prior days of accumulation. The desk's leverage data shows BTC open interest at $2.15 billion on OKX with funding annualized at 3.1%, still positive but moderating; liquidations over the past two hours totaled $277.9 million in BTC longs against $98.6 million in shorts. On the day, BTC is up 0.45% to $75,930.07, but down 5.48% over the week and down 39.1% from its 12-month high of $124,739.81. ETH is up 0.29% at $2,404.57 on the day but down 4.35% over the week and down 48.7% from its 12-month high. Stablecoins grew 1.09% over 30 days to $309.5 billion. The desk's Whale Watch board shows $164.6 million in ethereum and $3.4 million in bitcoin moving net onto exchanges over the past 48 hours, the largest single inflow being $76.9 million of bitcoin to Binance and $73.8 million of ethereum to Coinbase Institutional.

Zcash community governance polls closed September 14 with 2.4 million ZEC voting 99.9% to cut block times from 75 to 25 seconds and 98.9% to preserve Bitcoin-style halving cycles every four years, rejecting a smoothed issuance model. The block-time reduction would triple transaction throughput; formal ZIP consensus activation begins now, with implementation and network activation dates still to be determined. Separately, Balancer's governance forum posted a protocol shutdown proposal on September 14 to wind down operations and distribute its $9 million treasury to BAL token holders in staged redemptions from May 2027 to July 2028. Monthly protocol revenue stood at $30,000 in August against burn of $150,000, crossing the $60,000-per-month threshold set in April's restructuring that would trigger a governance review. A Snapshot vote is scheduled for September 25-29; if approved, the first redemption window opens May 31, 2027. Other infrastructure news: Solana's Transaction V1 mainnet upgrade increased transaction size limits from 1,232 to 4,096 bytes, enabling multi-step trades and privacy proofs in single atomic operations. Kamino, a Solana lending protocol with $1.352 billion in total value locked and $1.022 billion in active loans, appointed Michael Weisz, co-founder of Yieldstreet, as CEO on September 15 to lead institutional growth and U.S. market expansion from a new New York headquarters; Kamino ranks seventh among lending protocols tracked by DefiLlama, representing 2.7% of the category's $50.4 billion total.
